rule.title: Vulnerable HackSys Extreme Vulnerable Driver Load
rule.author: Nasreddine Bencherchali (Nextron Systems)

es.summary: Se cargó en el kernel el HackSys Extreme Vulnerable Driver (HEVD), un driver vulnerable a propósito que se usa para practicar explotación a nivel de kernel. Fuera de un laboratorio, indica un probable intento de escalar privilegios o de ejecutar código en el kernel.
es.what_it_detects: Eventos de carga de drivers (Sysmon Event ID 6) donde ImageLoaded termina en \HEVD.sys o el campo Hashes contiene uno de dos IMPHASH conocidos de HEVD 3.0. El IMPHASH detecta el driver aunque lo hayan renombrado.
es.why_it_matters: HEVD trae fallas de kernel documentadas a propósito. Un atacante con derechos de administrador puede cargarlo para ejecutar código en el kernel, desactivar defensas o llegar a SYSTEM. En ATT&CK corresponde a T1543.003: crear o modificar un servicio de Windows para persistencia y escalamiento de privilegios.
triage_steps: Revise ImageLoaded y Hashes. Una ruta distinta de HEVD.sys con IMPHASH coincidente indica que renombraron el driver para ocultarlo.
Verifique Signed, Signature y SignatureStatus. Si el driver no está firmado o tiene firma de prueba, compruebe si el host está en modo testsigning (bcdedit).
Busque el servicio de kernel que cargó el driver: evento 7045 del System log o claves en HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services en el mismo host ±15 minutos.
Identifique el proceso y el usuario que crearon el servicio, por ejemplo sc.exe create type= kernel, un loader propio o PowerShell, y revise su proceso padre.
Investigue la actividad posterior: procesos que pasan a SYSTEM desde una sesión de usuario, EDR o antivirus detenidos y nuevos usuarios administradores.
Confirme con el responsable del activo si es un equipo de laboratorio, CTF o capacitación, y busque alertas anteriores del mismo host o usuario.
false_positives: Laboratorios de explotación de kernel, cursos o CTF que usan HEVD de forma legítima y documentada.
Investigadores de seguridad o red team autorizados que prueban exploits en máquinas virtuales dedicadas.
response_steps: Si no hay una justificación documentada, aísle el endpoint de la red y preserve la evidencia: copia del driver, hash, memoria y registros.
Después de recolectar la evidencia, detenga y elimine el servicio del driver, borre el archivo y desactive testsigning si estaba habilitado.
Considere comprometido el host a nivel de kernel. Lo más seguro es reinstalarlo desde una imagen confiable y restablecer las credenciales usadas en él.
Bloquee los hashes del driver con WDAC o una política de bloqueo de drivers, y habilite HVCI donde se pueda.
es.severity_rationale: El nivel alto se justifica porque HEVD no tiene uso legítimo en producción y su carga permite ejecutar código en el kernel con privilegios máximos.

en.summary: The HackSys Extreme Vulnerable Driver (HEVD), a deliberately vulnerable driver used for kernel exploitation practice, was loaded into the kernel. Outside a lab, this points to a likely privilege escalation or kernel code execution attempt.
en.what_it_detects: Driver load events (Sysmon Event ID 6) where ImageLoaded ends with \HEVD.sys or Hashes contains one of two known HEVD 3.0 IMPHASH values. The IMPHASH still catches the driver after it is renamed.
en.why_it_matters: HEVD ships with documented, intentional kernel bugs. An attacker with admin rights can load it to run kernel code, tamper with defenses or reach SYSTEM. In ATT&CK this is T1543.003: creating or modifying a Windows service for persistence and privilege escalation.
triage_steps: Check ImageLoaded and Hashes. A path other than HEVD.sys with a matching IMPHASH means the driver was renamed to hide it.
Check Signed, Signature and SignatureStatus. If the driver is unsigned or test-signed, find out whether the host has testsigning enabled (bcdedit).
Find the kernel service that loaded the driver: System log event 7045 or HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services keys on the same host within ±15 minutes.
Identify the process and user that created the service, such as sc.exe create type= kernel, a custom loader or PowerShell, and review its parent process.
Look at what happened next: processes that move from a user session to SYSTEM, stopped EDR or AV, and new admin accounts.
Ask the asset owner whether the host is a lab, CTF or training machine, and look for earlier alerts on the same host or user.
false_positives: Kernel exploitation labs, courses or CTFs that use HEVD legitimately and have it documented.
Authorized security researchers or red teamers testing exploits on dedicated virtual machines.
response_steps: If there is no documented reason for the load, isolate the endpoint and preserve evidence: a copy of the driver, its hash, memory and logs.
After collecting evidence, stop and delete the driver service, remove the file and turn off testsigning if it was enabled.
Treat the host as kernel-compromised. Reimaging it from a trusted image is the safest option. Reset credentials that were used on it.
Block the driver hashes with WDAC or a driver blocklist policy, and enable HVCI where possible.
en.severity_rationale: High fits because HEVD has no legitimate production use and loading it gives kernel-level code execution with the highest privileges.

positive.description: HEVD.sys loaded from a user-writable folder via a newly created kernel service
HEVD renamed to look like a legitimate driver, matched only by IMPHASH

negative.description: Legitimate signed Microsoft driver load with an unrelated IMPHASH
Driver whose name only resembles HEVD (does not end with \HEVD.sys) and has a different IMPHASH
